title: How to Automate Commission Collection on Every Transaction
summary: Learn how to automate platform commission on every transaction, from setting split rules to handling refunds, without invoicing your sub-merchants.
body_markdown:
Commission is how most platforms make money. A marketplace takes a share of every order, a booking engine charges a fee per reservation, and a SaaS platform earns a cut of each payment it processes for its users. Yet many platforms still collect that money after the fact, by sending invoices to the businesses they serve and waiting to be paid.


That wait is expensive. Overdue invoices affect an average of


[44% of B2B credit sales across Asia](https://atradius.us/knowledge-and-research/reports/b2b-payment-practices-trends-asia-2025) , according to the 2025 Atradius Payment Practices Barometer, and bad debts average around 5%.


This guide explains how to automate platform commission so it is collected at the moment each payment settles. In this article, the businesses that sell through a platform are called sub-merchants, and the platform's own account is the master account.


Key takeaways


- Invoicing sub-merchants for commission turns platform revenue into receivables that may arrive late or not at all.


- Automatic deduction collects platform commission as each payment settles, before funds reach the sub-merchant.


- Commission rules should flex by sub-merchant, payment method, and number of parties without rebuilding the integration.


- Refunds and disputes need a clear policy, because automated commission does not always reverse on its own.


## Manual invoicing vs. automatic deduction


There are two basic ways to collect platform commission. With manual invoicing, the full payment goes to the sub-merchant, and the platform bills them later for its share. With automatic deduction, the platform's share is taken out of each payment before the rest reaches the sub-merchant.

The gap widens with scale. Invoicing ten sub-merchants a month is a chore. Invoicing a thousand means a finance team spends its time chasing money the platform has already earned. Atradius notes that late B2B payments in Asia are driven not only by customer liquidity but also by inefficient internal payment processes, a problem that manual commission collection only adds to.


## **How automated commission collection works**


Automating platform commission does not require a new business model. It moves the commission step from the finance team's month-end routine into the payment flow itself.


1. **Set the rule once.** The platform defines its commission as a percentage, a flat amount, or both, and assigns it to a sub-merchant or a group of them.


2. **The customer pays the sub-merchant.** The payment is recorded against the sub-merchant's account, so the sale stays in their name.


3. **The payment settles.** Once funds are confirmed, the commission rule runs automatically.


4. Commission moves to the master account.


The platform's share lands in its own balance, and the sub-merchant keeps the rest.


5. **Both sides see the same record.** Each deduction is linked to the payment that triggered it, so the platform and the sub-merchant work from one set of numbers.


The last step is what prevents disputes. When a sub-merchant can trace every deduction to a specific order, there is little left to argue about at month-end.


## How to set commission rules that scale


A single flat rate works on day one. As a platform grows, it usually needs more flexibility. Three situations come up often:


- **Different rates for different sub-merchants** .


A new sub-merchant might pay a promotional rate, while a high-volume partner negotiates a lower one.


- **Different rates by payment method** .


Card payments often cost more to process than bank transfers, so some platforms adjust their commission by method to protect their margin.


- **More than two parties.** A food delivery order may need to pay the restaurant, the rider, and the platform from a single payment.


The practical test is whether these changes can be made by updating a rule rather than rewriting code. On XenPlatform,


[split rules](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/split-payments) can be set as a flat or percentage amount, route one payment to several destinations, and apply different rates by payment method.


One detail is easy to miss: transaction fees are deducted from the account that receives the payment, so a split rule must leave room for them. A rule that tries to move 100% of a payment will fail.

## **What happens to commission when a payment is refunded**


Refunds are where automated platform commission needs the most care. When a customer gets their money back, someone has to decide whether the platform returns its share too.


There is no universal answer. Some platforms refund their commission in full, treating it as the cost of a good customer experience. Others keep it to cover their processing costs, or return it only for partial refunds. What matters is that the policy is written down, applied consistently, and explained to sub-merchants before they sign up.


The mechanics matter as much as the policy. On XenPlatform,


[split amounts are not returned to the source account automatically](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/split-payments) when the original payment is refunded. If the platform's policy is to return commission, it can move the amount back with a


[balance transfer](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transfer-balances) .


Timing helps too. If sub-merchants are paid out too quickly, a refund can arrive after their balance has already been withdrawn. A short holding period before payouts gives the platform room to settle refunds from the right balance.

## **Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)**


**What is platform commission?**


Platform commission is the share of each transaction a platform keeps for connecting buyers with sub-merchants. It can be a percentage of the sale, a flat amount per transaction, or a mix of both.


**Is platform commission the same as a platform fee?**


The terms are often used interchangeably. Some platforms use "commission" for a percentage of each sale and "platform fee" for a flat charge, but both describe the platform's share of a payment. What matters is that the term is defined clearly in your sub-merchant agreement.


**Can I charge different commission rates to different sub-merchants?**


Yes, if your payment setup supports per-account rules. On XenPlatform,


[split rules](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/split-payments) are assigned per payment and can use flat or percentage amounts, so platforms can apply different rates to different sub-merchants.


**Who pays the transaction fees when commission is deducted automatically?**


On XenPlatform,


[transaction fees are deducted from the account that receives the payment](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/split-payments) , and the split runs on what is left. Platforms that want to share fees differently can adjust their commission rate. Current rates are listed on the


[Xendit pricing page](https://www.xendit.co/en/pricing/) .


**Can commission be shared with more than one party?**


Yes. A single split rule on XenPlatform can route parts of one payment to several destinations, such as the platform and a delivery or logistics partner.


**Does automated commission work across currencies?**


Not on XenPlatform.


[Splits only happen in the same currency](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/split-payments) , with support for IDR, PHP, THB, VND, and MYR. Platforms operating in several markets set up commission rules per currency.
